alignments.note: Conjunction.
Rule 9: subject rides with the verb, headed on the lexical verb.
Participle.
The supplied expletive *There* is a rule 9 helper on the finite verb.
Rule 22: a substantival article whose complement is an adjective and not a participle keeps the discontinuous *he … that*, the copula going with the adjectival predicate under rule 53.
Rule 53: an adjectival predicate carries the supplied copula, headed on the adjective.
Genitive of comparison: *than* is the rule 7 helper the comparison licenses, headed on the pronoun.
Improper preposition rendered by a single English word (rule 71).
Pronoun.
The relative pronoun takes the ASV's *whose*; the resumptive αὐτοῦ is left empty rather than splitting one English word across two tokens.
Ordinary negative → *not*.
Rule 9: subject rides with the copula.
Predicate adjective; the ASV's own note glosses the Greek as *sufficient*.

The participle is rendered as the first English infinitive, so the infinitival *to* is its rule 7 helper and the idiomatic particle *down* rides with it. The competing reading gives *to* to λῦσαι, whose infinitive it formally is; I kept it on the word it introduces.
Rule 88: the supplied juncture *and* is a helper on the verb it introduces.
Rule 19: article → *the*.
Noun.
Rule 20: the determiner slot is occupied by the possessive *whose*, so the article realizes nothing.
Rule 21's determinerless clause: the case preposition *of* stays with the noun, discontinuously under rule 15.

The resumptive genitive pronoun has no English word of its own: the ASV writes a single *whose*, which I assigned to the relative οὗ that introduces the clause. Giving *whose* to αὐτοῦ and emptying οὗ remains defensible.

review_notes: οὗ … αὐτοῦ is a Semitic resumptive pair collapsed into one English *whose*; the note on each unit records which token I gave it to.
